name: Saltbox Colonial

revival_periods.note: A staple of the Colonial Revival cottage, and of Royal Barry Wills's practice, from the 1920s.

geography.hearth: eastern Massachusetts and the Connecticut River valley

lineage.note: The outshut or lean-to behind a two-storey range is an English medieval move; New England only had to make it universal.

description.short: A two-storey New England house with a single-storey lean-to across the rear, producing an asymmetric roof whose long rear slope runs almost to the ground.
description.long:
The saltbox is not a designed form. It is the visible record of a decision that thousands of families made independently: that the cheapest square footage in New England is under an extension of the roof you already have. A two-storey hall-and-parlor house needed more room — for a kitchen that could be got out of the hall, for a buttery to keep milk cool, for a borning room off the warm chimney wall. Building out the back at one storey and running the rafters down over it required no new plate, no new chimney and no second-floor framing. The result is a roof with a short front slope and a long rear catslide, a ridge that sits well forward of the plan centre, and a rear eave you can touch.

What the section does thermally is the reason the form persisted after it stopped being merely cheap. The long rear slope faces north in the standard siting, so the winter wind hits a surface it cannot get under and is deflected up and over; the low rear wall presents almost no elevation to it; and the unheated service rooms are stacked on the cold side, buffering the heated rooms from it. The house is, in effect, a windbreak with rooms inside. Once builders understood this, they began framing the lean-to from the start rather than adding it, which is why the distinction between integral and added lean-tos matters so much in the field. An added lean-to shows a pitch change at the original plate line, a break in the rafter run, and often a different sheathing; an integral one is a single unbroken slope from ridge to rear eave.

The front is the same face as any First Period house — five bays, central door, central chimney stack, small windows tight under the eave, riven clapboard — so the type is invisible from the road and obvious from the side. That asymmetry between the public and the working faces of the building is worth naming: the saltbox has one elevation for the world and three for the household, and it does not pretend otherwise.

Inside, the lean-to rooms feel entirely different from the front rooms. The ceiling follows the rafters down, so the far wall of the kitchen may be five feet high; the light is low and level, coming through small windows just above the counter; and the fireplace at the back of the central stack is the biggest one in the house, with the oven in its cheek. It is the room the family actually lived in, and it is the room the roof was extended to make.

defining_characteristics: Two full storeys at the front, one storey plus loft at the rear, under one continuous roof plane
Asymmetric roof: short front slope, long rear catslide, ridge set forward at 35–45% of the plan depth
Rear eave 6 ft 6 in – 8 ft 6 in above grade — low enough to reach
Central chimney stack serving front rooms and the rear kitchen fireplace, with the oven in the rear cheek
Lean-to depth 10–14 ft, holding kitchen, buttery and borning room
Five-bay symmetrical front with centre door; no corresponding order on the rear elevation
No dormers, and few or no second-floor openings on the rear slope
diagnostic_tells: From the gable end the roof is visibly lopsided — this is the only First Period type you can identify from a single oblique view
The rear eave is at head height while the front eave is at eighteen feet
A pitch change part-way down the rear slope means the lean-to was added; an unbroken slope means it was framed integrally
Rear windows are small, few, and set at odd heights because the ceiling is following the rafters
One chimney, dead centre, breaking the ridge forward of its midpoint

distinguished_from.difference: A Cape is one-and-a-half storeys with a symmetrical roof; a saltbox is two storeys in front with an asymmetric roof. A Cape with a rear lean-to is still a Cape — the front eave stays at nine feet.

A garrison is two full storeys front and rear with a framed overhang at the second-floor line and a symmetrical roof. Many garrisons later acquired lean-tos and became jettied saltboxes; the overhang is the deciding feature.

Revival saltboxes carry the asymmetric roof but give the rear slope dormers, full-height rear walls behind a false catslide, symmetrical windows on all elevations, an 8:12 pitch and an attached garage. If the rear eave is above ten feet, the section is fake.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The original two-storey frame governs; the lean-to is whatever the rafter can reach at the working pitch.
typical_ratios: Main body 38–42 ft × 18–20 ft; lean-to adds 10–14 ft of depth, total depth 28–34 ft
Ridge at 35–45% of total depth from the front wall
Front slope 45–52 degrees; rear slope 38–45 degrees if broken, equal to the front if integral
Front eave 16–18 ft above grade; rear eave 6 ft 6 in – 8 ft 6 in
Lean-to ceiling 7 ft 0 in at the wall of the main house, falling to 5 ft 0 in – 6 ft 0 in at the rear wall
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Five bays on the front, unequal, set by post positions with the narrow entry bay centred on the stack; the rear has no rhythm at all.

massing_affinities.note: The two-room core that the lean-to is added behind.
Half-house saltboxes exist, as at the Hoxie House.
A jettied two-storey front with a lean-to behind is a common hybrid.

constraints.statement: Rear eave height 6 ft 6 in to 8 ft 6 in above finished grade. Above 10 ft the catslide is cosmetic and the type is not present.

Front roof slope 45–52 degrees. Where the rear slope is broken it runs 38–45 degrees; where integral it matches the front exactly. A rear slope shallower than 35 degrees will not clear a usable lean-to ceiling.

test.note: Tests the front slope. The rear/catslide slope (38-45deg when broken, or matching the front when integral) is the statement's other, conditional claim and stays prose.

constraints.statement: No dormers on the rear catslide. The slope exists to shed weather and hold heat; puncturing it is the revival's habit, not the colonial one.
Lean-to depth 10–14 ft — the practical reach of a single rafter run past the plate. Beyond 14 ft the rear eave drops below head height at the door.

test.note: Reuses the general shed/lean-to depth concept.

constraints.statement: Sash 12/12 or 12/8 before c. 1750, 9/6 thereafter, with heads within 8 in of the front eave and no frieze band.

test.note: Tests the head-to-eave clause. The date-conditional sash pattern (12/12 or 12/8 before c.1750, 9/6 after) is OQ 22 territory and stays prose.

exemplars.name: Hoxie House
exemplars.note: A two-and-a-half-storey half house with an integral rear lean-to; frequently called the oldest house on Cape Cod, and a saltbox rather than a Cape despite its location.
exemplars.why: The saltbox a visitor to Cape Cod is shown first: the node's own note says it is 'frequently called the oldest house on Cape Cod'. (An earlier version also quoted a Wikipedia list the record does not cite; dropped at the 4 Sep audit rather than a ref typed from memory.)

exemplars.name: John Quincy Adams Birthplace
exemplars.note: Central-chimney saltbox with two rooms per floor flanking the stack; the lean-to was added c. 1764, so the rear slope shows the classic break. Often mis-dated to 1663 in popular sources.
exemplars.why: Well documented on both sides of the argument the node's own note raises about its date: the 1979 HABS data form (MA-597) gives the plan, the raised purlin roof and 'approx. 36' X 33'', while itself printing the 1663 date the node says is a popular error.

exemplars.name: Stanley-Whitman House
exemplars.note: A jettied saltbox — the type in its hybrid form, with a framed overhang on the front and a catslide behind.
exemplars.why: A type specimen of the hybrid the node's note describes -- a framed overhang in front and a catslide behind -- and a National Historic Landmark of 1960 whose Wikipedia description calls it 'a well-preserved saltbox with post-medieval construction features'.

exemplars.name: Boardman House
exemplars.note: Unusually unaltered First Period frame with an integral lean-to; the framing is legible throughout.
exemplars.why: The frame to measure rather than the facade to admire: the node's own note calls it 'unusually unaltered' with the framing 'legible throughout', Historic New England says it is unaltered from the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and HABS MA-492 drew it.

exemplars.name: John Adams Birthplace
exemplars.note: The plainer and older of the two Adams saltboxes, 75 feet from the other on the same property; built c. 1681 as a two-room central-chimney house, its purlin roof later raised on the north to take the lean-to. The 1897 restoration stripped the brick nogging from the studs, so the frame the 1979 HABS team measured is the survivor of a restoration as much as of a century.
exemplars.why: Measured by the 1979 HABS team at 41'-8" x 42'-5" with its lean-to, and the survey names the brick-nogged stud walls and the raised purlin roof, so it is the plain specimen whose figures can be read rather than the famous one next door.

exemplars.name: Hyland House
exemplars.note: A five-bay saltbox on the Connecticut shore, built 1713 for Isaac Parmelee: stone central stack, clapboard, diamond-pane sash symmetrical about a simply framed door with a five-light transom, and the rear roof face carried down to the first floor. Its chamfered girts are held to be an early example of that decoration -- the one carved decision, made carefully. A museum since 1918.
exemplars.why: The Connecticut shore's version, described by Wikipedia in the node's own terms -- five bays, a stone central chimney and the rear roof face extended to the first floor 'giving the house a classic New England saltbox profile' -- with chamfered girts held to be an early example of that decoration.

sources: Abbott Lowell Cummings, The Framed Houses of Massachusetts Bay, 1625–1725 (1979)
J. Frederick Kelly, Early Domestic Architecture of Connecticut (1924)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)
Dell Upton and John Michael Vlach, eds., Common Places: Readings in American Vernacular Architecture (1986)

proportion_packs.note: Inherits new-england-colonial's bay-generated frame in full -- same 16-20 ft bay, same central-stack logic -- and adds the one framing move that defines this variant: the lean-to is a NEW, shorter frame leaned on the main block's rear plate, not an extension of the main bay. This pack's wing_strategy rule (module x 0.8, giving 12-16 ft against the 16-20 ft main bay) sits close to this node's own recorded lean-to depth of 10-14 ft, and the pack states the mechanism in almost these words: 'this is why the saltbox reads the way it does: the rear lean-to is a shorter span leaned on the main frame's rear plate, and the catslide roof is the honest consequence.' The diagnostic distinction this node leads with -- a break in the rafter run means an added lean-to, an unbroken slope means an integral one -- is a fact about framing sequence, not about style, and this is the pack that explains it. As on new-england-colonial, no facade-system pack is bound: the front is generated by post position exactly as there, and the rear has no composed rhythm at all, being 'one elevation for the world and three for the household' in this node's own words.

The front roof follows the main block exactly as new-england-colonial (45-52 degrees, rafter length set by the 16-20 ft bay). The rear catslide is a second, independent structural decision: where it is integral the same rafter run simply continues past the plate at the same pitch; where it is added, a second and shallower run (38-45 degrees) is framed against the existing wall -- two different framing histories producing the same silhouette, which is exactly this node's own point about reading the break rather than the roof shape. The very low rear eave (6 ft 6 in - 8 ft 6 in) follows directly from this pack's near-zero eave allowance for First Period work: there is no boxed overhang to lift it, so the rafter foot is close to being the wall's top.

Governs the front openings on the same date sequence as new-england-colonial -- 12/12 or 12/8 to c. 1750, 9/6 thereafter -- which is this node's own co-occurrence constraint (c05) stated as a dating rule.

Bound for the single head-datum rule only, matching this node's own c05 (heads within 8 in of the front eave, no frieze). Not bound for its 13:6 window ratio, which this tradition's casement- and frame-set openings do not follow -- see new-england-colonial's binding for the same caveat.

The lean-to rooms are this pack's own 'service room' case by name: its service_zone_strategy rule (module x 0.8 = 11 ft 4 in) sits inside this node's recorded 8-11 ft lean-to breadth, and the pack calls that dimension 'one of the most characteristic dimensions in the whole vernacular catalogue' and names the saltbox directly as what it produces. Lean-to ceiling height is a section problem rather than a ratio -- the roof simply comes down to the rafters -- which the pack itself concedes when it says the governing dimension in a sloped space is the knee-wall head height, not a fraction of the storey below.
